newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: India declares victory at WTO conference.
newsitem.headline: India declares victory at WTO conference.

text.p: India had won most of what it wanted at the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) first ministerial conference here, a senior Indian official said on Friday.

Commerce Secretary Tejendra Khanna told reporters that while India had not been able to keep the highly sensitive issue of labour standards out of the WTO's final declaration, it had made sure its concerns were fully reflected.

"I think barring some unhappiness about the reference to two working groups on trade and investment, our brief has been faithfully adhered to by our delegation," Chidambaram told the parliamentarians.
Khanna, the commerce ministry's top official, told reporters at the WTO that ministers in Delhi had been briefed fully on what had happened in Singapore and "would reassure" parliament.
He said the WTO's closing declaration had said definitively that labour standards were the province of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and not the WTO.

But in New Delhi Finance Minister P. Chidambaram put a different spin on the labour issue. He told parliament's lower house India had won a key battle over international labour standards, but was not happy with a decision by the WTO on investment and trade competition.

Before he spoke, irate lawmakers had forced the abrupt adjournment of both houses of the Indian parliament and demanded a government statement on India's stance at the trade talks, accusing Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda of caving in to multinationals.
India had also begun the week by saying it would not allow mention in the final declaration of moves towards a multilateral investment agreement.
The final declaration, however, said the WTO would set up working groups to study the connections between trade and investment and trade and competition.

In contrast with Chidambaram, Khanna said that was not a cause for concern because the declaration stated explicitly that the studies would not form the basis for negotiations on a multilateral agreement.

It had also pledged that the 128 WTO members would not use trade measures to improve working conditions in the developing world which countries like India saw as a disguised attempt to undermine low-cost labour advantages, Khanna said.
"This is a very positive step because this was always lurking on the horizon," he said.
India began the five-day meeting on Monday by declaring it would not allow the labour issue on to the final declaration, which would mean that it became part of the WTO agenda.
Khanna said that the wording of the final declaration meant that objective had been won despite the subject being mentioned.
Khanna said there was no harm in a study, which might throw up ideas India could use in its own investment policies.
But he added: "We are not prepared to be told by anyone what our national investment policy will be. There is no question of India joining a consensus for negotiations. That question does not arise."
Khanna said India's view was similar on the WTO's agreement to launch a study of government procurement policies.
"This does not mean we are willing to open up any part of the Indian government's procurement," he said.

Srinivas Narayanan, India's ambassador in Geneva where the WTO is based, said Delhi had a positive attitude to the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) pact that was the highlight of the Singapore conference.
Pushed through by the United States, the ITA is designed to reduce tariffs on computer-related and telecommunications equipment to zero by 2000 and is likely to boost trade worth $600 million a year.
Narayanan said Delhi needed to study all the implications of the agreement before deciding whether to join it.
He said India had worries about the speed at which tariffs would be reduced to zero and on the products it covered.
"We need flexibility on the time frame and products," he added.
